name: sglang

facts.description: SGLang is a high-performance serving framework for large language models and multimodal models.

title: SGLang: A High-Performance Inference Engine for LLMs and Multimodal Models
answer: SGLang is an open-source serving framework for large language and multimodal models, maintained by the SGLang project under Apache-2.0. It sits at the inference and serving layer of the AI stack, handling deployment from a single GPU to distributed clusters with features like disaggregated prefill and decode, speculative decoding, and optimized GPU kernels. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that it is built for production-grade throughput and memory control rather than quick prototyping, and that its rapid release cadence means features and defaults change frequently.

sections.body: SGLang is a high-performance serving framework for large language models and multimodal models, made by the SGLang project and distributed under the Apache-2.0 licence. Its repository is sgl-project/sglang on GitHub, and its official site is sglang.io. The framework appeared as an open-source project and has since grown into a substantial codebase with tens of thousands of stars. In the AI stack it occupies the inference and serving layer, sitting between trained model weights and the applications that call them. It is not a training framework, although its blog describes training integrations such as RLinf's FSDP2 backend for fine-tuning. Its job is to take a model, whether a dense transformer or a mixture-of-experts architecture, and run it efficiently across one or many GPUs, exposing an API that applications can query. The site describes support from a single GPU to distributed clusters, and the release notes show ongoing work on parallelism, caching, scheduling and kernel optimization.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: SGLang is used for inference and serving of large language and multimodal models. Its model catalogue lists a wide range of architectures, including mixture-of-experts models with hundreds of billions of parameters, multimodal vision-language models, OCR models, text-to-speech and speech-to-speech models, and video generation models. The framework is strongest where throughput, latency and memory efficiency matter at scale. Its homepage highlights disaggregated prefill and decode, speculative decoding, parallelisms, a zero-overhead scheduler and optimized GPU kernels. Blog posts describe kernel-level work that lifted DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash decode throughput from 35 to 873 tokens per second, and day-0 support for new architectures such as Kimi K3. It is also used as an inference backend in training and evaluation pipelines, as shown by the RLinf integration with NVIDIA's Cosmos 3, where SGLang-Diffusion served as the backend and parallel evaluation throughput reached 3.33 times that of a straightforward integration. It is less obviously aimed at data preparation or classical machine learning, and the site does not present it as a training framework in its own right.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: SGLang is written in Python, so a working knowledge of Python is the first prerequisite. Beyond that, the material on the official site assumes familiarity with systems concepts: GPU memory, tensor parallelism, KV caches, attention mechanisms, quantization formats such as FP8 and FP4, and scheduling. The blog posts go deep into kernel optimization, CUDA graphs, and attention variants like MLA and KDA, which will be hard reading for someone without a background in deep learning systems. The site does not appear to offer a beginner tutorial track. Its homepage and blog are aimed at practitioners who already know how to run a model server and want to make it faster or cheaper. A student choosing what to learn should expect to need prior exposure to transformer inference and distributed systems before the documentation becomes useful, and should treat the release notes as the primary source for current behaviour rather than as an introduction.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around SGLang is visible in its model catalogue, which lists dozens of supported models from many vendors, including Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax and Thinking Machines. The site documents integrations with NVIDIA tooling such as FlashInfer, DeepEP and NIXL, and with transfer engines like Mooncake. It supports Hugging Face model loading, as shown by the RLinf adapter that treats Cosmos3 as an external Hugging Face model. Documentation lives on sglang.io, and the project runs a first SGLang Summit on November 12 and 13, 2026 in San Francisco, which indicates an active community. The GitHub repository is the centre of development, with a rapid stream of pull requests referenced in the blog, such as the Breakable CUDA Graph work published as #19102, #22218 and #27988. The site does not give detailed community support channels beyond this, so a reader should check the repository for issue trackers and discussion forums.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: SGLang is built primarily for production performance rather than quick experiments. Its feature set, including disaggregated prefill and decode, speculative decoding, hierarchical caching and custom kernels, is aimed at serving models efficiently under load. The blog posts measure throughput, time to first token and token hit rates, which are production concerns. That said, the framework does offer conveniences that help during development, such as a CPU-only simulator that runs the real scheduler, radix cache and hierarchical cache with a latency predictor in place of the model forward, predicting time to first token within about six percent on most traces. It also supports beam search by passing beam_width in a request, and returns sampling masks for inspection. The cost of this production focus is complexity: many optimizations are opt-in flags, such as --enable-layernorm-sp or --startup-weight-load-mode overlap, and defaults change between releases, so teams must track versions carefully.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts and the site show that SGLang is used by teams working with frontier-scale models. Its model catalogue includes trillion-parameter reasoning models, 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts models like Kimi K3, and multimodal systems, which suggests adoption among organizations serving very large models. The RLinf integration with NVIDIA's Cosmos 3 shows use in robotics and simulation pipelines. The project is actively developed, with a last push date in October 2026 and a summit announced for November 2026, so it is a current choice rather than a legacy one. For someone choosing it for work, that means skills in SGLang are relevant to current inference infrastructure roles, though the site does not list specific employers or job titles. The rapid pace of change also means that knowledge of its internals dates quickly, and the site does not claim any formal certification or training programme.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: SGLang is written in Python and is typically used alongside PyTorch-based model definitions, Hugging Face model weights, and NVIDIA GPU libraries such as FlashInfer, DeepEP and trtllm_mla. It integrates with training frameworks like RLinf, which uses FSDP2, and with transfer engines like NIXL and Mooncake for moving KV caches between prefill and decode workers. The polyglot pattern it belongs to is one where Python orchestrates serving and scheduling while lower-level kernels and communication libraries handle the performance-critical work. The site describes kernel work in terms of CUDA graphs, GEMM tile sizes and quantization formats, which implies that C++ and CUDA components sit underneath the Python surface. It is not presented as a replacement for training frameworks or for general-purpose web frameworks, but as the serving layer that those systems call into when a model needs to answer requests at scale.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: SGLang's weaknesses follow from its focus. It is complex to operate, with many opt-in flags and defaults that change between releases, and the site does not provide a beginner-friendly path into that complexity. Some features are explicitly immature or in flux: the /v1/responses endpoint no longer retains results in memory unless the server starts with --enable-response-store, and without it retrieval and chaining return errors, which is a behavioural change that could surprise existing users. The blog describes optimizations that are measured on specific hardware and model shapes, so their gains may not transfer. The official material does not say how stable the API is across versions, what the project's long-term governance looks like, or how it compares directly with other serving runtimes. It also does not state minimum hardware requirements or give a clear support policy, so those questions remain open for a reader evaluating it.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
